question: Is it haram to play board games, chess or games with dice with one's family?
asked: During the lockdown, to entertain the children and pass the time, my family and I play board games, and sometimes those games involve dice. I came across a fatwa on a popular Islamic Q&A website saying it is haram to play board games with dice with one's family, because there is a hadith that forbids this.
answer:
He mentions the website name, but we shall not mention it. It is a very popular website that answers Q&A about Islam. And my advice or suggestion is that it might have some good, but really people should stick with the scholars of their own lands or countries. Even if it's not any... find people within your own locality and ask them. Sometimes these websites are based in one land, and there's a lot of cultural connotation that is not suitable for other lands.

So this response, and again, I remind the viewers that this is the shortened version. I know that, as usual, you're going to have refutations and people are going to have other opinions, but this is the reality of fiqh, subhanAllah. I'm not the first to say what I'm about to say. Nonetheless, this is the shortened response.

Yes, there is a hadith that forbids something called nardashir. The Prophet said, in the hadith in Sahih Muslim, "Whoever plays with nardashir, it is as if he has dipped his hands in pig's blood and in pig's flesh." So this is a hadith that is very explicit. Now, there are a number of issues involved over here. What exactly is nardashir? And is it applicable to the game or to the dice? Because again, the issue comes: how do you interpret this word here?

The word nardashir is a Persian word, and it is actually a reference to the game that has now evolved into backgammon. There was a rudimentary version of backgammon back then that the Persians had invented (nardashir is a Persian word), and they had this game of backgammon that they would gamble with. And backgammon, to this day, is sometimes played as something that people bet their money on, and the winner basically takes it all. So nardashir primarily applies to backgammon. Now, there are some versions or some reports that might reference the dice as well. But the more authentic version, of Sahih Muslim, says nardashir, and nardashir is primarily applied to the game of backgammon. Now, some have said that the prohibition is of the dice itself, and there is some basis for that: how do you separate the game? It is all put together.

As well, there are some reports about the game of chess. Now, there's nothing authentic from the Prophet about chess, shatranj, but there are a number of reports from the Sahaba and Tabi'un that some of them disapproved of chess, somewhat rather harshly. And it is also reported, by the way, that some of them did not disapprove of chess. If you look up Sunan al-Bayhaqi, one of the great books of hadith, there is an entire chapter about what people have said regarding chess. And you will find a number of reports that are very harsh. Ali ibn Abi Talib, for example, basically said, "I wish I could throw this board game onto your face. Have you been created to do this?" He found a group of people all playing chess, basically surrounding a match and whatnot, and he became irritated, radiAllahu anhu.

And so you have some very strict statements from the Sahaba and Tabi'un, but you also have, on the other side, some of the Tabi'un and Tabi' al-Tabi'in of whom it is authentically narrated that they would actually play chess. And of them, Imam al-Shafi'i, rahimahullah ta'ala, says that Muhammad ibn Sirin and Hisham ibn Urwa would play chess in private. It means it's not something they would publicize; it's not something you do in front of everybody, but with your family or in the privacy of the room, and they would just go, just a little bit of time to pass, to play chess. And Ibn Abd al-Barr says in his Tamhid that it is reported from Ikrimah and al-Sha'bi that they would play with the nard. And Sa'id ibn al-Musayyib was asked about playing with the nardashir, and Sa'id ibn al-Musayyib, the great, great Tabi'i, the famous Tabi'i, said: if there is no money or gambling involved, then there is no problem with it.

Now, these are some reports from these great Tabi'un and Tabi' al-Tabi'in. I want you to know, this is my short response; I'm not going into detail. You will find more reports from the Sahaba, Tabi'un and Tabi' al-Tabi'in that are disapproving. So there's no question; I'm not trying to hide that. But you want a response, I'm going to give you a simple response. You will find a longer list of people who disliked it, but these are great scholars who basically said it's okay with certain conditions.

And the position that I'm advocating is that we need to be a little bit more pragmatic and take a look at the broader picture. Those respected and great ulama (some of them are my teachers, and I respect them immensely), those that say that all types of games and cards and board games and dice and everything is haram, I fully understand, I fully sympathize, because in their minds they want the Ummah to reach the highest level. And the fact of the matter is, as Ali radiAllahu anhu said, were you created to do this? No, you were not created to spend hours and hours playing board games and doing chess and whatnot. We have a higher purpose.

But when you look at the status of the Ummah, this is something that the books of fiqh call ma ta'ummu bihi al-balwa: everybody is doing it now, everyone is doing it. So for us to adopt the strictest position essentially means nobody cares what we say, and it's as if you are speaking to a wall, because you can say whatever you want. And with my utmost respect, the very people who are giving this fatwa, because I know the reality, their own families, their own children, maybe even they themselves, cannot live up to this fatwa perfectly. And when that is the case, then really you need to take a step back, because the Sharia is never going to be impractical. The Sharia has always applied.

And if this is the case, you also realize that we're living in a time and a place where, again, let us be frank here, there are far bigger problems for our children than them sitting down to play a board game, than them sitting down to play chess. The stuff that they're watching on television, a'udhu billah; the Netflix that they're watching, a'udhu billah; the online entertainment and whatever, TikTok, all of these things out there. And so you're going to come and say that if a father and mother and children sit down and play ludo, or cards, or a game of chess, or whatever amongst themselves, just to pass the time, that is haram and forbidden and sinful in the eyes of Allah? There is no evidence from the Qur'an and Sunnah to make that sinful at all. Yes, there's a hadith that talks about backgammon, but the question is: is the prohibition because of the gambling, which is what I am saying and what these Tabi'un said, or is it just any type of board and any type of game involving dice and whatnot?

And if you look at it really, to me at least, it is very obvious what the fatwa is that we need to give to the people. Look, I'm being precise here, so pay attention to this. There is no question that we have a higher purpose in life than to spend hours and hours playing video games or watching TV or doing something of this nature. And not all of these things I mentioned are at the same level. Some of them are sinful in what we see or what we hear. Some of them are mubah, permissible. But the mubah, when it is done too much, becomes makruh, and when it leads to haram, it becomes haram. So even the mubah is like salt: you add it to the food.

And so my position, the fatwa I'm going to give you, is that all of these board games and chess and the dice that is used for non-gambling... As for gambling, by unanimous consensus: when you put money (we're talking about real money; Monopoly is not real money, right?), so we're talking about when you put money and people are betting and they have games and whatnot, there is no question that any type of game that involves money, actual money, and is based upon the luck of the draw, or the luck of the cards, or the luck of the dice, that is absolutely haram. There should be no two opinions about that.

As for when there is no gambling involved, then my suggestion, my advice, is that families should understand that indeed we do have a higher purpose, and that we have a problem across the board of wasting too much time in entertainment, in movies, in all that we do. So it's not just the dice and the games; it is overall. We are killing time, and we have not been created to kill time. We have been created to be productive with our time. Nonetheless, you cannot continuously, 24 hours a day, do something that is absolutely productive. The mind needs to take a break; the body needs to take a break. Your children cannot be expected to be... constantly. They're going to play; they're going to do what they're going to do.

And therefore, if we use this like salt, just a little bit, once in a while, and we sit down... And for the adults especially, for the parents especially, my advice to you all is: when you sit down with your children to play these games, your niyyah should be not the game, but family time. Your niyyah should be: I want to come closer to my children, my spouse, my kids. I want to teach them manners. What should you say? What should you do? Even as you play a game, you can bring in some benefits, some fawa'id. Rather than using vulgarities, say something beneficial. Remind them of their past, their heritage, your family history. Teach them something that is beneficial, even of this dunya.

So the goal should not be the game. The goal should be quality time with the family, and the game is an excuse for the kids to come, because they don't want to listen to you. And when you make that niyyah, insha'Allah, I actually think it's not only just mubah; you might even be rewarded. If you actually intend to do something productive and useful with your family, to teach them something of benefit, then as you sit down with them and play a board game or whatnot, insha'Allah it might even be an act of worship. At the very least, we can say it is mubah.

But a number of points. First and foremost, this should not take up most of your time or day. And as you grow older, you need to cut back. And I speak now especially to the young men: O young men in college, you need to stop playing your PS4s and Xboxes ten hours a day. That's not going to benefit you. You're no longer five years old or ten years old. When you get to your 30s, what are you doing, half the time playing this game? No, definitely at that stage you need to cut back and be reasonable. I understand, all of us need a bit of a break. We all have different breaks. Some people take breaks reading esoteric books of history, but that's beside the point. Some people like to take these types of breaks. I understand; it is in and of itself mubah, but do not make it the bulk of your time. What is reasonable varies from person to person as well.

Make sure that you do not do anything haram within it, because there are some... not board games (well, maybe there are some), but there are some video games that have vulgarities in them, or where you're expected to do blatant haram. And parents, it is your job to...

So here's the point. Those people who say it's haram to play board games: okay, you say that. What are the kids going to do? The parents think it's haram; no child is going to listen to this fatwa. They're going to be in their rooms watching their TikToks, doing their PS4 games and whatnot. And so again, isn't it better to take the children out of their private bedrooms and bring them to the living room with the parents, instead of them watching what they shouldn't, instead of them playing games where the characters are doing things that are indecent or violent or gory? Because that's the alternative, right? The parents are going to be following a fatwa way up there; the children are not going to be doing that.

So, as you're aware if you listen to me, I don't believe in abstract fatwas. Fatwas have to benefit the ummah. We have to teach and preach at the level of the ummah. And to make these types of things haram, I really think that it is harmful to the ummah to be this strict. I understand if we're talking to a group of, mashaAllah, huffaz in the madrasa, full-time students of Islamic 'ilm: for sure, for them we can be a little bit stricter and say, "Hey guys, why are you doing something of this nature? Do something more productive. Don't spend hours and hours." But to give a blanket fatwa of this nature, that all types of board games or all types of amusements are haram? No. It is like salt: you do it a little bit, and the goal should be family time. The niyyah should be spending quality time.

And also, playing a board game with the children is infinitely better than the children being in their rooms doing the games or watching the movies that they should not be doing. So it is better to do this; it is definitely the lesser of the two evils. **And therefore, inshaAllah, there is no sin on you whatsoever if these conditions are met.** And again, as the kids grow older, also try to do this less and less, and do something more productive more and more. And Allah subhanahu wa ta'ala knows best.
